all_in_channel.description: Threads in a Slack channel only. If true, list every Routine in this channel, including other threads' and ones that start a new session each time they fire. Default false.

cursor.description: Opaque pagination cursor from a previous response's next_cursor. Omit for the first page.

enabled.description: When set, only Routines whose enabled state matches. true hides fired one-shots, paused, and auto-disabled Routines; false shows only those. Omit for both.

include_completed.description: If true, also include one-shot Routines that have already fired (e.g. delivered send_later reminders) and Routines moved to a project. Default false — there can be thousands.

recurring.description: When set, filters by schedule shape: true keeps only cron-driven (recurring) Routines, false only one-shot and fire-only Routines. Omit for both.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__read_documentation
tools.description: The documentation for the machine and product this session runs in: a claude.ai cloud container and the settings around it (GitHub access, connectors, the environment's secrets, network access, setup script and installed tools, the session's limits and permission prompts, Remote Control). Read it whenever something about your container or environment comes up, whether it blocked you, you worked around it, or the person asked how to set it up. For example: the repository the work is about is not in your container, a clone or push is refused, a service you need has no connected connector, an outbound host is denied, a command-line tool is missing, you need an API key, the person asks how to stop permission prompts. Read it rather than answering from memory because these settings move and get renamed faster than your training data, and a page says what is true now: the current steps, where in the product the person makes the change, and what you can do yourself. Reading a page also helps the person directly: in the Claude Code app they see a card with a button that takes them to that settings page, so they can fix it themselves while you carry on. Call it with no topic to list the pages and when each applies; call it with a topic to read that page. Read a page each time a different topic comes up; one read per topic is enough. It is read-only and needs no approval. It has nothing on bugs in the code you are working on.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__send_later
tools.description: Schedule a message to be delivered back into THIS SESSION at a future time. The message arrives as an ordinary user turn, so you can use it to remind yourself to resume work, check on something, or continue after a delay. Delivery survives container restarts. Granularity is one minute — the scheduler polls every minute, so sub-minute precision is not available. This is a thin wrapper over create_trigger (a self-bind + run_once_at Routine); the returned trigger_id can be passed to delete_trigger to cancel before it fires, and the Routine disables itself after firing once.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__subscribe_pr_activity
tools.description: Subscribe this session to GitHub activity on a pull request. Once subscribed, comments, reviews, CI results and other PR events are delivered into this conversation as <wake reason="external-event"><event source="github" ...> envelopes. This tool call is idempotent. Use this when asked to autofix, monitor, watch, or babysit a PR. A PR's events go to one session at a time. If the tool result says a Claude agent is already watching the PR, the call succeeded but this session will not receive events: another conversation's Claude session, or a Claude agent that labels the PRs it watches, holds them. This session can take over only once that one stops: it unsubscribes or ends, or its watching label is removed from the PR.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Code_Remote__update_trigger
tools.description: Update a Routine's (scheduled trigger's) name, cron expression, enabled state, model, or prompt. Only provided fields are changed; omit a field to leave it as-is. The Routine must belong to this account — updating another account's Routine fails with not-found. Use list_triggers to find the trigger_id if it's no longer in context. A Routine that REQUIRES A COMPUTER (its trigger shows a bound_device) is special: its name, schedule and enabled state change freely, but a new prompt takes effect only when the person approves this call in a Cowork conversation linked to that same computer (their approval re-signs the prompt for it) — otherwise the result is status: needs_device_approval and NOTHING is changed, which is not an error to work around: tell the user, and never delete and recreate the Routine (that loses its run history and the computer it requires). Send schedule/name/enabled changes in a call WITHOUT a prompt so they are not held back by it. Its model cannot be changed from here at all.

cron_expression.description: New 5-field cron expression. Fields without a prefix are UTC. If you know the user's time zone, write the fields in their local time after CRON_TZ=<IANA time zone> and a space (weekdays at 8:52am in Los Angeles: CRON_TZ=America/Los_Angeles 52 8 * * 1-5). When a recurring schedule (run_once_at is unset) at a fixed time of day would land on the hour or half hour (a plain '9am' or '9:30'), prefer using a jittered minute value instead. Most schedules run on minute 0, so runs scheduled at those times can be delayed due to server traffic. By default, move the time 1 to 15 minutes earlier (for '9am', 8:45 to 8:59); use the number of letters in the task's name, modulo 15, plus 1. Leave midnight, a time on any other minute (e.g. 9:10) and a run that must follow an event as asked. Setting this clears run_once_at (and any ended_reason).

When in doubt, ask the user first. Only fires that create a new session pick up the new model; a Routine bound to a persistent session (self-bind or persistent_session_id) keeps that session's model until the binding clears. content.content:
# The report and the record

## What every report holds

Your brief says where your report goes: a file that it names, your final message, or both. If it names no file, your report is your final message.

A finding is something that your work learned about the tree or the language, and that the record does not hold yet. Examples: a defect, a behaviour that departs from the specification or from a decision of the curator, a measurement. What you did along the way is not a finding, for example the files that you read or edited. Your transcript keeps that.

A point to report is a kind of change or finding that the curator wants to review. Your brief names its points to report. Examples: a changed line of a test that the team wrote, a checker edit inside a change to the library, a changed line of the model program.

Put each of these that you have in your report, in this form, whatever else your brief asks for:

- **Defects.** Each defect that you measured, and the test or ledger row that records it (`tests-writing.md`, "How a defect is recorded").
- **Sentences of the specification made false.** Each sentence of the specification that your change makes false, quoted with its file and line. Such a sentence says what walk or the compiled path does. It is in the effect of an Appendix I entry (`Specification/appendices/changes.tex`), or in a `\revision` or `\note{}` box beside a passage.
- **Decisions.** Each choice that you made among alternatives, as a decision apart from the findings: what you chose, the alternatives, and the evidence, cited. If no decision of the curator covers it, say so, and say which reading you acted on. A decision left as a line inside the findings counts as not made.
- **Points to report.** Each point that your brief names and the work reached, with its evidence, also one that only part of the work reached.
- **Commands.** Each command that you had to work out because this skill does not give it, with what it does.
- **Questions for the curator.** If something needs the curator's decision, list it as a decision not taken, in the form that `exploring.md` gives. The reader of your report brings it to the curator. Do not choose which of your items anyone reviews.

## At a point to report

- If the work reaches a point to report, do what the brief says for it. For example, a brief can say that a defect in the code is recorded in a ledger row and not repaired.
- Then finish the work.
- If a step cannot be undone, or would change a decision of the curator, report it instead. List it as a decision not taken, with its alternatives.

## Timings and citations

- If you take a timing that you will keep, run nothing else beside it. All agents of the session share the machine's cores (the `cloud-container` skill).
- Name the machine with every timing: `nproc`, the CPU's model and MHz, the load at start, the JDK, `FORTRESS_THREADS`. Only a pair of timings taken in one run measures a difference.
- If you take a measurement again because the code changed, say what changed.
- In a report, cite the tree at file:line, and quote results, two to five lines, each with its command. Never cite a file under `tmp/`.

## POSITIONS and FACTS

POSITIONS and FACTS describe the present: no dates, no names of who found what, no "corrected" or "superseded" notes. The history of each entry is in `POSITIONS-history.md` and `FACTS-history.md`, beside them.

A FACTS entry is the fact, its source and its test in a few lines, under a bold title. It points to the report that holds the detail. Cite it by its bold title, or by its opening words if it has no title.

## The gap ledger

The ledger's rows are the bug reports that the work fixes. A fix of a row starts with its reproduction, written as a test (`tests-writing.md`).

A row is one line of eight cells, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of a topic section. Reports cite a row by its number, which it keeps for good. A new issue gets a new row.

- Its status is one of seven words: `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`, `CONTESTED`, `RETIRED`, `FIXED`, `DUPLICATE`. The last three close a row. The row template (below) defines each.
- Its class is a kind and an area, such as `implementation gap (checker)`.
- The earlier text of a changed row is in `explorations/fortress-gap-ledger-history.md`.

Read the ledger only through the queries below: it is too large to read whole.

## Reading the record

Read only the slice of the record that you need. This tool prints whole entries, in parts of bounded size:

    T=explorations/coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh

- `$T 'positions:WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints one of the curator's decisions. Run it before you choose among ways to do something. If several titles hold the words, it names them.
- `$T 'WORDS OF A TITLE'` prints each FACTS entry whose bold title holds them, and `$T 'section:HEADING'` every entry of a FACTS section. Run one before you investigate a behaviour of the tree, and when your brief or a note names an entry. These queries and `positions:` read titles only: before you write that the record does not hold something, also grep FACTS and POSITIONS for its words.
- `$T 'index:WORDS'` prints the INDEX lines that hold the words. Run it to find the notes on a topic.
- `$T 'ledger-find:WORDS'` prints one line for each ledger row that holds every word. Run it when you meet a defect, before you investigate it.
- `$T 'ledger:ROW'` prints one row whole. Run it for each row that you need from a find, your brief or a note.
- `$T 'doc:PATH#HEADING'` prints a section of any note, or of a `.tex` chapter, and `$T 'map:FILE#HEADING'` a section of a note under `explorations/coordinator/map/`. Run one when your brief or a note names a section. `#HEADING@WORDS` prints only the table rows and list items of that section that hold every one of WORDS.
- `$T --check QUERY ...` prints only where each query matches and its size. Run it before a query whose size you do not know. `--part N` prints part N of a long output, and `--help` gives the rest.

A word of a query that ends in `*` matches the start of a word. Any other word matches a whole word.

Before you edit a file of the original tree, list the ledger rows that cite it, and read each row that your edit can change:

    python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py find --cites FILE

## Writing to the record

- Add a fact to FACTS in the commit that establishes it, as a new entry in the section of its topic. Its source and its test can be the code at file:line, a gated test, or a command and its output. If your brief does not let you write FACTS, put the entry in your report as finished prose.
- Rewrite a wrong line of FACTS in place.
- POSITIONS holds the curator's decisions, in the curator's words, written once. Everything else points there. Write a decision there only if your brief gives it to you to record. If you have evidence against one, do as `exploring.md` says.
- Put new files of the work under `explorations/`. If you add a note directly in `explorations/` or `explorations/reviews/`, add its line to INDEX: ``- `PATH`: `` and the first sentence of the note's header comment.

Write the gap ledger only with `ledger.py`, which checks each line that it writes against the row template.

    L="python3 explorations/coordinator/tools/ledger.py"

To add a row:

1. Print the row template, about 3 KB: `$T 'doc:explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md#The row template'`.
2. Write the row as one line in a file under your tree's `tmp/`, with `?` in its number cell.
3. Run `$L add FILE --section TITLE`. It numbers the row and puts it in that section. If the row breaks the template, it adds nothing and prints each rule broken. `$L sections` lists the titles.

To change a row:

- `$L note N TEXT` adds TEXT to the notes of row N.
- `$L duplicate N --of M` makes row N a pointer to row M.
- `$L close N --commit HASH --test NAME` marks row N `FIXED`, by the commit HASH and its test NAME. Run it once that commit is in `HEAD`, and commit the close after it.

## The repository's history

- The repository is a 2018 fork of `sirinath/fortress`, a git conversion of the project's java.net Mercurial repository. Its trunk runs from 2007-01-04 to 2012-08-31 and ends at `a874948ac`, the team's last commit.
- The commits after `a874948ac` are the revival's. After the tag `sealed-tree`, commit `75cca6683`, the revival began to fix the team's code, test first. Before it, the revival changed mainly the build and the toolchain.
- `git diff a874948ac -- FILE` shows what the revival changed in a file, and `git diff 75cca6683 -- FILE` what it changed after the tag.
- The conversion cut 146 parent links, so a `git log` of a directory stops at a cut and misses the team's earlier commits. Use `git log --follow` on a file, or compare contents.
- To find who wrote something, or where the repository's history after 2012 comes from, read `research/authorship.md` and `explorations/coordinator/lineage.md`.

# Committing and pushing

**scratch**
: Files and folders that your work makes and `main` does not keep: logs, captured and raw run output, copies of tools, probe programs, lists and private caches folders.

Your brief says whether you commit and push, and on which branch. If it says nothing, commit on your current branch, and push it.

## What to commit

- Commit your change, its tests, your report if it is a file, and any reusable script.
- Commit what you write to the record, such as a ledger row, with the work that it records. A row's close follows the fix's commit (`records.md`).
- Keep scratch in your tree's `tmp/`, which is gitignored.
- In a fresh clone, `.claude/worktrees/` and `.claude/agents/` show as untracked, because the lines of `.git/info/exclude` that hide them are not in the clone. Do not commit them.
- Keep a copyrighted PDF or deck in `research/decks/`, which is gitignored. Cite it by its Wayback URL. Notes on it go in `research/extracts/`: your own summary, with brief attributed quotations.
- Put provenance and rationale in commit messages and reports, not in source comments.

## How to commit

Commit as you go, each commit in one command that names its paths:

    git add -- <paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <paths>

- The command commits only the paths that it names. Other agents may have uncommitted edits in your tree. Leave them alone.
- If you renamed a file with `git mv`, name its old path in `git commit` only, because `git add` refuses a path that no longer exists: `git add -- <new paths> && git commit -m "<message>" -- <new paths> <old paths>`.
- Never commit a copied directory, and never use `git add -A`.
- Before you commit more than a few hundred lines, stage them and read what you staged: `git add -- <paths> && git diff --cached --stat -- <paths>`.
- If the commit edits the original tree, say so in its message.
- End every commit message with this footer, exactly, whatever footer Claude Code suggests:

      Co-Authored-By: Claude <noreply@anthropic.com>
      Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_01AmiXNpJxQ6TBwec4vJZHDB

  If your brief gives another session line, use it.

## Pushing

Push after every commit, so that a lost container loses nothing.

- If you work on your own branch, push it: `git push -u origin <branch>` the first time, then `git push`. Your brief says how the branch reaches `main`.
- If you work on `main`, other agents commit to it too. Push only your own commits:
  1. Run `git log origin/main..main`. Your commits are those whose hashes your own `git commit` printed.
  2. If it lists another agent's commit, run the command again shortly: that agent pushes right after it commits. If the commit stays, push nothing, and say so in your report.
  3. If it lists only your commits, push three times, in this order:

         git push origin main
         git push origin main:claude/worker-brief-fable-vnnuv8
         git push origin main:blinded-fable

     The third push keeps `blinded-fable` current. If the container is lost, the platform rebuilds it from that branch.
- Push no branch that this section does not name, unless your brief names it.
- If a push is refused, push nothing more, and say so in your report.

34	## 1. What the paper is
35	
36	The abstract claims "the first formal specification of a strongly typed
37	object-oriented language with symmetric multiple dispatch, multiple
38	inheritance, and parametric polymorphism with variance", with a static and a
39	dynamic semantics and a type soundness proof "demonstrating that our novel
40	dynamic dispatch algorithm is consistent with the static semantics"
41	(p. 11:1). The calculus is **FGFV**, "Featherweight Generic Fortress with
42	Variance" (p. 11:3). It formalises the overloading rules of the 2011 OOPSLA
43	paper (Allen et al., in the tree as `Papers/Types/`), which were stated
44	informally and without a language semantics. It adds declaration-site
45	variance and a dispatch algorithm, and proves that the static rules and the
46	run-time choice agree (§6, p. 11:25).
47	
48	The language (Fig. 2, p. 11:8; §3.2, pp. 11:8-9):
49	- **Traits and objects.** Traits are "like Java interfaces that do not have
50	  any fields", and objects are "like Java final classes that cannot be
51	  extended".
52	- **Type parameters.** Trait type parameters carry a variance mark (`+`, `-`,
53	  `=`) and upper bounds. Object type parameters are always invariant. Method
54	  type parameters have lower and upper bounds, and the defaults are `Any` and
55	  `Bottom`.
56	- **Expressions.** Variables, first-class functions, object creation with
57	  written type arguments, and method calls `e.m(e)` with no written type
58	  arguments.
59	- **Types.** `Bottom` "is intentionally not expressible in the surface
60	  syntax" (p. 11:9). Union and intersection types exist only as internal
61	  types (p. 11:9). Tuples are not values.
62	- **What is left out.** "FGFV omits functional methods … and declarations
63	  of closed types …, but these could be added back to FGFV in an obvious
64	  way" (p. 11:3). Related work adds "modularity, nominal exclusion, and
65	  closed types" to that list (p. 11:25). There are no top-level functions:
66	  what is overloaded is methods.

68	## 2. The rule excluding multiple instantiations
69	
70	- **The rule.** Every pair of a class's proper ancestors must satisfy
71	  [Anc-Diff-Trait] (instances of two different traits: no condition) or
72	  [Anc-Same-Trait] (Fig. 4, p. 11:11). [D-Trait] and [D-Object] both check it
73	  (Fig. 3, p. 11:10). [Anc-Same-Trait] requires that "if a class C extends two
74	  instances of a trait T, T⟦α⟧ and T⟦ρ⟧, then C also extends some T⟦γ⟧
75	  (which may be T⟦α⟧, T⟦ρ⟧, or a third instance) that extends both"
76	  (p. 11:11).
77	- **Per variance (our derivation from the rule's two subtype premises).** An
78	  invariant parameter forces γ = α = ρ, so two different instances cannot
79	  both be ancestors: that is the blanket rule. A covariant parameter needs an
80	  ancestor instance whose argument is below both arguments, and a
81	  contravariant one needs one whose argument is above both.
82	- **Why.** "Because the rules guarantee that there always exists a single
83	  minimal ancestor when a class extends multiple instances of a trait, no
84	  ambiguous method calls are possible due to multiple instances of a trait"
85	  (p. 11:11).
86	- **Credited.** The discussion calls it "the 'Ancestor Meet Rule' …
87	  introduced into Fortress in 2012 by Guy Steele and David Chase … to design
88	  an expressive type system with union and intersection types". It gives the
89	  laws T⟦α ⊓ α′⟧ ≡ T⟦α⟧ ⊓ T⟦α′⟧ for a covariant T and T⟦α ⊔ α′⟧ ≡ T⟦α⟧ ⊓
90	  T⟦α′⟧ for a contravariant one, and not "the 'obvious other two cases'"
91	  (p. 11:24). The citation is "Personal communication".
92	- **Used by the overloading check.** To close part of the gap between
93	  subtyping of domains and inclusion of applicable sets, the checker reduces
94	  an existential domain by collecting the constraints that keep it from being
95	  `Bottom` (*existential reduction*, pp. 11:13-14). The worked case uses
96	  invariance: with `ArrayList` extending `List` and both invariant, subtypes
97	  of `ArrayList⟦P⟧` and `List⟦Q⟧` "are exclusive unless they are both
98	  ArrayList⟦S⟧ for some type S" (pp. 11:13-14). So the rule is what lets
99	  two generic declarations be proved disjoint or nested.
100	- **Not argued.** The paper argues that the rule is sufficient, not that it
101	  is necessary.

103	## 3. Variance
104	
105	- **Subtyping.** Declaration-site variance on trait type parameters, as in
106	  the example "T⟦U2, U1, U1⟧ <: T⟦U1, U2, U1⟧" for `trait T⟦+P, -Q, =S⟧` with
107	  U2 <: U1 (p. 11:9).
108	- **Positions.** [D-Method] checks that covariant and contravariant class
109	  type parameters appear only in positions of their own variance. A *type
110	  context* gives each position a variance: arrow domains and contravariant
111	  arguments flip it, and "type parameters of objects and invariant type
112	  parameters of traits are invariant" (pp. 11:11-12).
113	- **The overloading rules do not change.** "The overloading rules for FGF
114	  remain the same because covariant or contravariant types affect only the
115	  well-formedness of method declarations rather than the validity of
116	  overloading" (p. 11:12).
117	- **Run time is where variance costs something.** "Supporting variance in a
118	  type-sound manner requires keeping track of the static types of method
119	  invocations at run time" (p. 11:7).
120	  - The example: `sort(x: ListC⟦A⟧)`, `sort(x: ListC⟦B⟧)` and
121	    `sort⟦P⟧(x: ListC⟦C⟧): SortedListI⟦P⟧`, with `ListC` covariant and
122	    `SortedListI` invariant, beside a generic
123	    `merge⟦P⟧(SortedListI⟦P⟧, SortedListI⟦P⟧)`.
124	  - Two calls statically typed `SortedListI⟦A⟧` feed a merge. If run time
125	    instantiates the third `sort`'s `P` as anything but `A`, "the merge call
126	    would fail, despite the fact that the program successfully passed static
127	    type checking" (p. 11:7).
128	- **The 2012 alternatives.** The team considered dropping contravariance,
129	  treating arrow domains as invariant and compensating "by introducing rules
130	  of coercion". They also considered dropping union types, and perhaps
131	  intersections, for pseudo-joins and pseudo-meets. The paper instead
132	  accepts "the potential for exponential blowup" at run time (p. 11:24).

134	## 4. How dispatch picks among overloads
135	
136	### 4.1 The static rules (§4, pp. 11:12-15)
137	
138	- **The reading of a generic declaration.** Following Allen et al. 2011, a
139	  generic declaration is "a single declaration whose domain type is
140	  existentially quantified over its type parameters", not "a set of
141	  infinitely many monomorphic declarations" (p. 11:3). "A monomorphic method
142	  declaration is a generic method declaration without any type parameter"
143	  (p. 11:5).
144	- **Specificity.** The informal rules compare applicable sets, "which is not
145	  practically checkable", so the formal ones compare domain types by
146	  subtyping (p. 11:12). This is sound but "not complete" (p. 11:13), and
147	  existential reduction narrows the gap (§2 above).
148	- **Three rules for every pair of same-named declarations** (Fig. 5,
149	  p. 11:13):
150	  - No Duplicates: neither domain is below the other.
151	  - Meet: the domains exclude ([Meet-Excl], their intersection reduces to
152	    `Bottom`), or one is below the other, or a third declaration's domain is
153	    equivalent to their intersection ([Meet-Third]).
154	  - Return Type ([Return-Test]): when d1 is more specific than d2,
155	    `arrow(d1)` must be a subtype of `∀⟦κ, κ′⟧((α ⊓ α′) → ρ′)`, where the
156	    κ are both declarations' type parameters, α and α′ their domains and ρ′
157	    the less specific return type.
158	- **What [Return-Test] guarantees.** It checks the informal rule "for any
159	  instance of d2 instantiated with σ2 that is applicable to γ, there exists
160	  an instance of d1 … that is applicable to γ and has a return type that is
161	  a subtype of the return type of the instance of d2" (p. 11:15). That is,
162	  it quantifies over every instance of the less specific declaration.
163	- **Theorem 4.1** (p. 11:15). "For any method invocation, there always
164	  exists a unique most specific method declaration in its set of applicable
165	  method declarations." No Duplicates makes specificity antisymmetric, and
166	  the Meet Rule gives "a meet for every nonempty subset".
167	- **Static resolution** ([T-Method], [MSAV], Fig. 7, p. 11:16). The checker
168	  picks an instance of the most specific declaration applicable to the static
169	  argument types, and annotates the call with that instance's return type.
170	  The type-annotated expression `ϵ.m(ϵ): α` is what runs.
171	
172	### 4.2 The dynamic choice (§5.2, pp. 11:16-21)
173	
174	- **The contract.** "dynamic overloading resolution then must select an
175	  instance of the most specific method declaration that is applicable to the
176	  dynamic types of the arguments and whose return type is a subtype of the
177	  static type of the expression" (p. 11:15).
178	- **Types at run time.** Types are reified: "all the type parameters are
179	  instantiated with ground types at run time", and a value's run-time type is
180	  its *ilk* (p. 11:17). Ground types include unions and intersections
181	  (Fig. 8, p. 11:17).
182	- **[R-Method]** (p. 11:17). It sorts the visible declarations most-to-least
183	  specific ("This order is statically determinable, so the sorting can be
184	  done at compile time"). It then runs the *dispatch semipredicate* on each
185	  declaration in turn and takes the first that succeeds. The receiver's ilk is
186	  matched together with the arguments' ilks, which is what makes the dispatch
187	  symmetric.
188	- **The semipredicate** ([Dispatch], pp. 11:17-18) has three steps:
189	  1. match the argument ilks against the domain to get lower and upper bounds
190	     for the method type parameters;
191	  2. match the call's static return type against the declared return type to
192	     get bounds "to make sure that the dynamic dispatch preserves type";
193	  3. solve the bounds.
194	
195	  "If any of these steps fails, the semipredicate is false: the declaration
196	  is not applicable" (p. 11:18). Matching a union can yield several candidate
197	  bound lists, combined as a Cartesian product (pp. 11:18-19).
198	- **Solving** (Fig. 10, p. 11:19). The rule works from the rightmost type
199	  parameter to the left and "computes a substitution … by taking the
200	  intersection of the upper bounds", declared and computed. It then
201	  propagates the choice into the declared lower bounds of the parameters to
202	  its left. It "never instantiates method type parameters with Bottom". The
203	  right-to-left pass works because of the binding restrictions (p. 11:11):
204	  - a method type parameter's scope "extends to the right of its
205	    declaration";
206	  - "no reference to a method type parameter appears in any of the upper
207	    bounds";
208	  - the union of the lower bounds must be below the intersection of the upper
209	    bounds.
210	- **The worked example** (§5.2.4, pp. 11:20-21).
211	  - Two covariant `append` declarations, over `SortedList` and over `List`.
212	  - The call has static type `List⟦C3⟧` and argument ilks `SortedCons⟦C1⟧`
213	    and `Cons⟦C2⟧`, with C1, C2 <: C3.
214	  - The `SortedList` declaration fails on the second argument, so the `List`
215	    one runs, instantiated at `[C3/P, C3/Q]`.
216	  - So the instance comes from the static return type's upper bound, not from
217	    the ilks' C1 and C2.
218	- **Why intersection of upper bounds.** The Fortress team "had assumed …
219	  that once the tightest possible upper and lower bounds for a method type
220	  parameter have been found, then the union (or pseudo-union) of the lower
221	  bounds should be chosen". For that and for a hybrid "we were unable to
222	  complete the proofs of correctness", so the algorithm "always chooses the
223	  intersection of the upper bounds" (p. 11:25).
224	- **Union instances.** A type parameter can be instantiated at a union at
225	  run time. In the paper's example `O.m(3, true): (Int ⊔ Boolean)`, "P of m
226	  is inferred as (Int ⊔ Boolean) by the dispatch semipredicate at run time"
227	  (p. 11:21).
228	
229	## 5. The run-time check on the return type
230	
231	- **What it is.** Every call carries its static return type into run time
232	  (§5.1, p. 11:16). Dispatch uses it as an upper bound when it instantiates
233	  the chosen declaration (p. 11:18).
234	- **It never moves a call to another declaration.**
235	  - Lemma 5.8: whatever instance the checker chose, "there exists a
236	    type-safe most specific method instance at run time" (p. 11:22). Its proof
237	    is where [Return-Test] is used (pp. 11:22-23).
238	  - Lemma 5.9: the first-dispatchable scan then yields an instance of the
239	    most specific declaration applicable to the ilks, with a return type below
240	    the static one (p. 11:23).
241	  - In a well-formed program the return-type bounds therefore never rule out
242	    that declaration. They only choose its instance.
243	- **What it costs.**
244	  - "In simple invariant cases, we expect the run-time cost to be relatively
245	    low but nonzero", since matching `List⟦String⟧` against `List⟦T⟧` only
246	    binds T (pp. 11:24-25).
247	  - For the covariant and contravariant cases, "caching or dynamic
248	    recompilation … may help" (p. 11:25).
249	  - The discussion calls left-to-right scoping "a relatively small sacrifice
250	    of expressivity for a large gain in dynamic efficiency" (p. 11:24).
251	
252	## 6. What it proves and what it leaves open
253	
254	**Proved (sketched here, full proofs in the companion report):**
255	- Theorem 4.1: a unique most specific declaration exists (p. 11:15).
256	- Soundness and completeness of type matching and of solving (Lemmas 5.1 to
257	  5.4), and so of the dispatch semipredicate (Theorems 5.5, 5.6;
258	  pp. 11:21-22). Completeness of matching assumes that a matched type holds
259	  no `Bottom` and no type parameter inside a union or intersection. The
260	  paper shows that every use meets this: declared types have neither, and
261	  unions reach a declaration only through already-ground instances
262	  (pp. 11:21-22).
263	- Lemmas 5.7 to 5.9 (pp. 11:22-23).
264	- Theorem 5.10, soundness of a method call: a well-typed call is reduced by
265	  [R-Method] and its body's type is below the call's static type (p. 11:23).
266	- Theorem 5.11, type soundness: if `e` types to `(ϵ, д)` and `ϵ` evaluates to
267	  a value, the value's type is below `д` (p. 11:24).
268	- Only the method-invocation case is proved, "the other cases are
269	  conventional" (p. 11:23). The proofs are not mechanised; the Coq model in
270	  the lineage is Kim and Ryu 2011, without generics (p. 11:4).
271	
272	**Left open or left out:**
273	- No static inference algorithm: "we do not present a specific static type
274	  inference algorithm that finds the substitution σ in rule [E-Sub]". The
275	  paper conjectures that its match rule could serve (p. 11:25).
276	- Domain subtyping is incomplete against applicable sets (p. 11:13).
277	- Exponential blowup is possible at run time (p. 11:24).
278	- The union-of-lower-bounds instance is unproved (p. 11:25).
279	- Functional methods and top-level functions, closed types (`comprises`),
280	  nominal exclusion (`excludes`) and modularity are out; the paper says they
281	  "could be added back … in an obvious way" but shows nothing (pp. 11:3,
282	  11:25). Self types and a numeric tower are absent: neither is mentioned,
283	  and `Integer` appears only in a `List⟦Integer⟧` example (p. 11:2).
284	- Method type parameters may not appear in upper bounds, so F-bounded method
285	  parameters are outside the calculus (p. 11:11). Trait parameters' bounds are
286	  checked in an environment that binds the parameters themselves ([D-Trait],
287	  p. 11:10), so by the rule's form F-bounded trait parameters are admitted.
288	- Whether the ancestor rule is necessary is not argued.

291	
292	The paper cites neither text; its only 2012 source is "Steele and Chase 2012.
293	Personal communication" (p. 11:28). The lineage is by content.
294	
295	**Welterweight** (`Papers/Welterweight/`: "Dynamic Dispatch and Type Inference
296	Semipredicates", Chase, Hilburn, Luchangco, Naden, Ryu, Steele, Tristan,
297	"PAPER SUBMITTED TO 2012 ACM SPLASH---OOPSLA", `paper.tick:499-509`; Naden

302	  - the Ancestors Meet Rule and its reason, a "unique minimal instance" for

304	  - ilks;
305	  - the most-to-least-specific order with a first-success scan of dispatch

310	  - **Inputs to dispatch.** Welterweight dispatches on the ilks alone: it is

339	- *Kept:* the Return Type Rule, plus multiple instantiation exclusion: "any

14	The record's account (`literature.md` § 1) was right as far as it went: the paper keeps the invariant-instantiation exclusion through its ancestor rule, moves the return-type check to run time, and has no self types and no numeric tower. What it did not have, each checked in the text:
15	
16	- The instance rule. "The Fortress team had assumed, because it seemed from several working examples to be in accord with intuition, that once the tightest possible upper and lower bounds for a method type parameter have been found, then the union (or pseudo-union) of the lower bounds should be chosen as the type to be used for that type parameter. We considered this and the hybrid technique ... but we were unable to complete the proofs of correctness of both the techniques. Since the minimum requirement for a type to instantiate a method type parameter is that it satisfies all the lower and upper bounds of the type parameter, the dynamic dispatch algorithm presented here always chooses the intersection of the upper bounds." (§ 5.4, p. 11:25, lines 1274-1284.) The rule itself is [Solve-Step] (§ 5.2.3, p. 11:19, lines 965-1016): the substitution for a parameter is the intersection of its computed upper bound and its declared upper bounds, checked against the lower bounds; "Because g' is a ground type, the solving step never instantiates method type parameters with Bottom."
17	- The static return type at run time. Dispatch "seeks the most specific method declaration with a dispatchable instance that is applicable to the ilk of the arguments and whose return type is a subtype of the annotated static return type" ([R-Method], § 5.2.1, p. 11:17, lines 888-896); "the language semantics needs to make the static types of method invocations available at run time" (§ 2.3, p. 11:7, lines 329-331). The upper bound of a return-only parameter comes from that static return type ([Dispatch], line 875: `g match ρ - bounds`).
18	- The default bound. "By default, each type parameter has an upper bound Any and a lower bound Bottom" (§ 3.2, p. 11:9, lines 418-419). `Bottom` "is intentionally not expressible in the surface syntax" (line 438).
19	- The overloading rules in checkable form (§ 4, Figure 5, p. 11:13, lines 630-661): No Duplicates as non-subtyping of domains either way; Meet as exclusion, subtyping or a third declaration whose domain is equivalent to the intersection ([Meet-Third], line 645); Return Type as one universal subtyping check, `arrow(d1) ⊑ ∀[κ,κ']((α ⊓ α') → ρ')` ([Return-Test], lines 656-660). Specificity is subtyping of existentially quantified domains, "a sound approximation of the subset relation of applicable sets, [but] not complete" (§ 4.2, p. 11:13, lines 673-675), narrowed by "existential reduction", which collects the constraints that keep a domain off `Bottom` and solves them (lines 733-743, Figure 6).
20	- A restriction the proof needs. A method's type parameter bindings are well formed only if "no reference to a method type parameter appears in any of the upper bounds" and every reference falls within a left-to-right scope; "restriction (1) makes dynamic dispatch more efficient and restriction (2) makes it consistent" (§ 3.3, p. 11:11, lines 565-570); the one-pass right-to-left solve depends on it (lines 1010-1016, 1258-1262). Trait type parameters carry no such restriction.
21	- What the calculus leaves out. "FGFV omits functional methods [Allen et al. 2007] and declarations of closed types [Allen et al. 2011], but these could be added back to FGFV in an obvious way" (§ 1, p. 11:3, lines 142-144); "FGFV does not support features like modularity, nominal exclusion, and closed types in their work, [but] they can be added in an obvious way" (§ 6, p. 11:25, lines 1302-1303). No coercion, no `nat` parameters, no numbers.
22	- The exclusion rule's form and date. [Anc-Same-Trait] (Figure 4, p. 11:11, lines 530-532): a class extending two instances of a trait must extend an instance below both; "the 'Ancestor Meet Rule' ... was introduced into Fortress in 2012 by Guy Steele and David Chase" (§ 5.4, p. 11:24, lines 1230-1232). For an invariant parameter only the same instance is below both; for a covariant one the lower instance is.
23	- Variance in full: marks `+ - =` on trait parameters, objects always invariant (§ 3.2, lines 406-409); a covariant parameter only in covariant positions, a contravariant one only in contravariant ones ([D-Method], § 3.3, pp. 11:11-12, lines 571-595); dispatch with variance marks (§ 5.2.2); exponential blowup only where union types meet contravariance, accepted (§ 5.4, lines 1239-1257); the two alternatives the team weighed in 2012, dropping contravariance or dropping union types.
24	- Cost. "In simple invariant cases, we expect the run-time cost to be relatively low but nonzero"; for variant cases "caching or dynamic recompilation" (§ 5.4, pp. 11:24-25, lines 1263-1273).

Polymorphic Symmetric Multiple Dispatch with Variance

GYUNGHEE PARK, KAIST, South Korea and Oracle Labs, USA
JAEMIN HONG, KAIST, South Korea
GUY L. STEELE JR., Oracle Labs, USA
SUKYOUNG RYU, KAIST, South Korea
Many object-oriented languages provide method overloading, which allows multiple method declarations with
the same name. For a given method invocation, in order to choose what method declaration to invoke, multiple

(such as mathematical operators) intuitively and consistently, it is difficult to guarantee that calls will be

Functional method declarations can overload with function declaraions.
A valid overloading between a functional method declaration and
a function declaration is
determined by applying the (more restrictive) Meet Rule for functions
to both declarations.

\section{Declarations with Static Parameters}
\seclabel{overloading-static-params}

The rules above compare the parameter types and the return types of
declarations without static parameters.
A declaration with static parameters is read as one declaration whose parameter
type ranges over every instance of it whose static arguments satisfy their
bounds (\secref{overloading-terms}).
A declaration $d_1$ is more specific than a declaration $d_2$ when $d_2$ is
applicable to every call to which $d_1$ is applicable, and not the other way
round (\secref{resolving-overloading}); where neither has static parameters,
this is the relation $\Ps \strictsubtype \Qs$ of the rules above.
A set of overloaded declarations, some or all of which have static parameters,
is a valid overloading when every pair $d_1$, $d_2$ of them satisfies the
following three rules:
\begin{itemize}
\item
The \emph{No Duplicates Rule}: $d_1$ and $d_2$ are not each more specific than
the other.
\item
The \emph{Meet Rule}: $d_1$ and $d_2$ exclude each other, or one of them is more
specific than the other, or some declaration of the set is more specific than
both and applicable to every call to which both are applicable.
\item
The \emph{Return Type Rule}: if $d_1$ is more specific than $d_2$, then for
every argument type other than \TYP{BottomType} to which $d_1$ is applicable,
and for every instance of $d_2$ that is applicable to it, some instance of $d_1$
is applicable to it whose return type is a subtype of the return type of that
instance of $d_2$.
\end{itemize}
The Subtype Rule, the Incompatibility Rule and the Meet Rule above are these
rules for declarations without static parameters, with the conditions that
coercion adds; the Return Type Rule is the Subtype Rule's condition on return
types, checked over every instance of the less specific declaration and not
over one instance chosen for the pair.

As in \secref{more-specific-rule}, declarations of the set that are each more
specific than both $d_1$ and $d_2$ and that together cover every argument to
which both are applicable also satisfy the Meet Rule.
\revision{revival-meet}{The type group's paper of 2011 states the Meet Rule
without this case.}

Two parameter types with static parameters exclude each other, for the Meet
Rule and the Incompatibility Rule, as the type group's paper of 2011 decides it
by \emph{existential reduction}: each static parameter stands for any type
within its bound, and where the two parameter types mention one parameterized
trait, instantiation exclusion (\secref{trait-types}) lets them meet only where
the static arguments of those mentions are the same, every static argument but
an operator argument counting.
So where \TYP{Box} and \TYP{Pair} are distinct object types with static
parameters, the parameter types \EXP{\TYP{Box}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket} and
\EXP{\TYP{Pair}\llbracket{}A, B\rrbracket} of two declarations exclude each
other whatever \VAR{T}, \VAR{A} and \VAR{B} stand for.

The Return Type Rule refuses the following pair, where trait \TYP{Round}
extends trait \TYP{Shape} and object \TYP{Circle} extends \TYP{Round}:
%(* Not allowed! *)
%ident[\T extends Shape\](x: T): T = x
%ident(x: Round): Round = x
\begin{Fortress}
\(\mathtt{(*}\;\hbox{\rm  Not allowed! \unskip}\;\mathtt{*)}\)\\
\(\VAR{ident}\llbracket{}T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Shape}\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)\COLON{}T = x\)\\
\(\VAR{ident}(x\COLON \TYP{Round})\COLON \TYP{Round} = x\)
\end{Fortress}
The second declaration is more specific than the first.
For an argument of type \TYP{Circle}, the instance of the first at \TYP{Circle}
is applicable and returns a \TYP{Circle}, but the second, which runs for such an
argument, returns only a \TYP{Round}, and it has no other instance.
The pair is allowed when the second declaration is itself generic:
%ident[\T extends Shape\](x: T): T = x
%ident[\T extends Round\](x: T): T = x
\begin{Fortress}
\(\VAR{ident}\llbracket{}T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Shape}\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)\COLON{}T = x\)\\
\(\VAR{ident}\llbracket{}T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Round}\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)\COLON{}T = x\)
\end{Fortress}
Its instance at any type to which it is applicable returns that type.
\revision{revival-overloading}{This section is new.
The Working Draft of February 2011 required overloaded declarations to have
identical static parameters and ignored them.
The rules stated are those of the type group's paper of 2011 (Allen, Hilburn,
Kilpatrick, Luchangco, Ryu, Chase, and Steele, ``Type Checking Modular Multiple
Dispatch with Parametric Polymorphism and Multiple Inheritance'', OOPSLA 2011),
which the compiled type checker applies, with its Return Type Rule checked over
every instance of the less specific declaration; the pair refused above has the
shape of that paper's own example, which the compiled path used to accept and
then fail to verify.
Neither implementation runs the pair allowed above today: the interpreter
refuses it at load, since it asks two declarations with static
parameters for a pair of parameter types that exclude each other (row~159 of the
revival's gap ledger), and the compiled code generator fails on it (row~537).
The compiled implementation adds one restriction that is not a rule of the
language.
When one declaration with static parameters is more specific than another that
declares as many static parameters of its own, the two must declare them of the
same kinds, position by position, and the return type of the more specific one
must be a subtype of the other's when their static parameters are identified
position by position; for its code generator hands the static arguments that a call writes,
by position, to whichever declaration the call dispatches to (row~398 of the
revival's gap ledger).
So it refuses this override, whose return type names its static parameters in
the other order, where \TYP{Pr} is an object with two type parameters:
%trait Maker
%  make[\A, B\](): Pr[\A, B\]
%end
%object M extends Maker
%  make[\A, B\](): Pr[\B, A\] = Pr[\B, A\](1)
%end
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{trait} \TYP{Maker}\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \VAR{make}\llbracket{}A, B\rrbracket()\COLON \TYP{Pr}\llbracket{}A, B\rrbracket\)\-\\\poptabs

sortJP <: AK(x: ListI JP K): SortedListI JP K = · · ·

Defining a provable system for an object-oriented language requires addressing various technical
challenges due to the structural asymmetries inherent in the language design. One can have a
variable of type Any, but one cannot have a variable of type Bottom. The ilk of an actual argument
must be a subtype, not a supertype, of the method’s parameter type. The ilk of a returned value

recompilation in reaction to the relative frequencies of types actually encountered may help.

language asymmetries described above and trying to understand their consequences. In particular,
the Fortress team had assumed, because it seemed from several working examples to be in accord
with intuition, that once the tightest possible upper and lower bounds for a method type parameter
have been found, then the union (or pseudo-union) of the lower bounds should be chosen as the
type to be used for that type parameter. We considered this and the hybrid technique of using the
intersection of upper bounds only when the union of lower bounds is Bottom, but we were unable
to complete the proofs of correctness of both the techniques. Since the minimum requirement for a
type to instantiate a method type parameter is that it satisfies all the lower and upper bounds of the
type parameter, the dynamic dispatch algorithm presented here always chooses the intersection of
the upper bounds.

necessary substitution σ to satisfy the rule [E-Sub] for existential subtyping during static analysis.
This is more difficult than the corresponding calculation during dynamic dispatch because at run
time one always matches an ilk (which contains no type parameters) to a type, but at compile time
one must match a type against a type, where each type may contain type parameters. Indeed, we do
not present a specific static type inference algorithm that finds the substitution σ in rule [E-Sub],
but only refer to previous work in this area. However, we conjecture that the match rule presented
here can serve this role after being extended to handle the case of matching two type parameters.

## The row template

A row is one line of eight cells, `| # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |`, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of its topic section, in number order. A pipe inside a cell is written `\|`. (POSITIONS, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md`, section 4.)

- **#**: the row's number, the next free one when it is added; never reused, renumbered or given to another row. 148 is vacant.
- **claim**: at most 300 characters, whose first 150 name the defect or the capability: what fails or what holds, and where.
- **status**: exactly one word of seven, with no second status and nothing in brackets:
  - `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`: it works; it ran and its output is recorded.
  - `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`: the specification settles it and the reproducer confirms it. A row with one half fixed stays `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, and its notes say which half is fixed.
  - `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`: the failure reproduces; the mechanisms tried are named and are not exhaustive.
  - `CONTESTED`: unsettled; the notes say why.
  - `RETIRED`: a source's claim falsified here, kept so that it is not derived again.
  - `FIXED`: closed by a landed commit (`ledger.py close`): the claim's first sentence, the test as reproducer, notes `fixed HASH; full text: history, row N`.
  - `DUPLICATE`: a pointer (`ledger.py duplicate`), notes `duplicate of row M; full text: history, row N`.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Check a consolidation of FACTS.md or POSITIONS.md: every entry of the file as
it stood at BASE appears verbatim, whole, in the file now or in its history file,
and in exactly one of the two.

An entry is a top-level bullet ("- ") with its indented continuation lines.
Written 2026-09-27 for the POSITIONS split (886a06e1d, repaired in cda7d86a6,
whose first pass had lost 20 entries' text); generalised 2026-09-29 to either file.

usage: check-verbatim.py BASE FILE HISTORY
  e.g. check-verbatim.py 8c1158937 explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md explorations/coordinator/FACTS-history.md
Exit 0 when no entry is missing and none is in both files; 1 otherwise.
"""
import subprocess, sys

if len(sys.argv) != 4:
    sys.exit(__doc__)
base, path, hpath = sys.argv[1:]
old = subprocess.run(['git', 'show', f'{base}:{path}'], capture_output=True, text=True, check=True).stdout
new = open(path, encoding='utf-8').read()
hist = open(hpath, encoding='utf-8').read()

def entries(text):
    out, cur, start = [], None, 0
    for i, ln in enumerate(text.split('\n'), 1):
        if ln.startswith('- '):
            if cur is not None:

Kim and Ryu [2011] presented three overloading rules: Exclusion Rule, Subtype Rule, and Meet
Rule. Every pair of method declarations with the same name must satisfy one of these overloading
rules. The authors proved that a set of overloaded method declarations satisfying the overloading
rules does not produce any ambiguous method invocation at run time.
   To understand the interplay between symmetric multiple dispatch and parametric polymorphism,
Allen et al. [2011] focused on a type system without any specific target language and informally
presented three other overloading rules: a No Duplicates Rule, a revised Meet Rule, and a Return
Type Rule, where every pair of method declarations with the same name must satisfy all three
overloading rules. The authors showed that interpreting a polymorphic method declaration as a set
of infinitely many monomorphic declarations is not appropriate for overloading resolution. Instead,
they considered a polymorphic method declaration as a single declaration whose domain type is
existentially quantified over its type parameters as proposed by Bourdoncle and Merz [1997].
   In this paper, we present a formal core calculus FGFV (Featherweight Generic Fortress with Vari-
ance) for an object-oriented language with symmetric multiple dispatch, multiple inheritance, and
parametric polymorphism with variance. For conciseness, FGFV omits functional methods [Allen
et al. 2007] and declarations of closed types [Allen et al. 2011], but these could be added back to
FGFV in an obvious way. Unlike the prior work, we formally present overloading rules for FGFV,
define its dynamic semantics with a novel dynamic dispatch algorithm, and prove type soundness.

The pages below were read from the PDF (its pages 10 to 22 are the article's 11:10 to 11:22; the figures are images), and the line numbers are the text file's. Nothing above this section is changed; where the full text overturns a sentence above, this section says so.

### 7.1 The rules at the source, claim by claim

- **Figure 5, the No Duplicates Rule (p. 11:13).** Three rules, any one sufficient: [No-Dup-Triv] for different names, [No-Dup-Not-Less], `¬(Δ ⊢ dom(d) ⊑ dom(d'))`, and [No-Dup-Not-Gtr], `¬(Δ ⊢ dom(d') ⊑ dom(d))`. The prose: "if the domain type of one declaration is not a subtype of the domain type of the other, they satisfy the rule ([No-Dup-Not-Less] and [No-Dup-Not-Gtr])" (p. 11:12, lines 609-611). So two declarations are duplicates exactly when their domains are each below the other. *Confirms* § 4's caveat, and *overturns* the extract's compression, "neither domain is below the other" (`ParkPOPL2019-extract.md:150`), which should read "not each below the other"; the extract is not among this check's files, so that is reported, not repaired.
- **Theorem 4.1 (p. 11:15).** "We first show that the more specific relation of method declarations is a partial order. It is clearly reflexive and transitive since the existential subtype relation is reflexive and transitive. The No Duplicates Rule guarantees that it is antisymmetric" (lines 784-786). *Confirms* § 4: antisymmetry is what the rule buys, and it needs exactly that no two distinct declarations have equivalent domains.
- **[D-Trait] and [D-Object] (Figure 3, p. 11:10).** Both begin `Δ' = Δ ∪ {{} <: P <: {ξ}}`, `distinct(P)`, `Δ' ⊢ ξ ok`: a trait's or an object's parameter bounds are checked under the parameters themselves. *Confirms* § 1, and extends it to the three storing objects: [D-Object] admits `T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }` on `__DefaultVector`, `__DefaultMatrix` and `TransposedMatrix` as [D-Trait] does on `Vector` and `Matrix`.
- **[Binding-Step] (Figure 4, p. 11:11), restriction (2).** `FV(χ') ⊆ parameters(Δ) ∪ {P}` and `FV(η') ⊆ parameters(Δ)`: a method type parameter's lower bounds may name the parameters to its left, its upper bounds may name only the class's parameters; the prose, "(2) no reference to a method type parameter appears in any of the upper bounds" (lines 565-570). *Sharpens* § 1: `pmul[\T extends { Number, MultiplicativeRing[\T\] }, nat k\]` fails the figure's premise at `T ∈ FV(η')`, not only the prose; the 38 are outside the theorem as stated. The bound of a method's own parameter is checked here, under [D-Method]'s premise `Δ ⊢ [[{ξ} <: Q <: {ξ}]] ok`, so § 1's parenthesis "(it is checked by [D-Trait])" holds for a trait parameter's bound only; the point it serves, that a bound is no position of the method's arrow type, stands.
- **[D-Method] (Figure 3, p. 11:10; p. 11:12).** The variance premise is on the arrow type alone, `(V = =) ∨ (∀T. ((τ → ω) ≠ T[P]) ∨ (Δ ⊢ T variance V))`, and the type context's fourth clause, "type parameters of objects and invariant type parameters of traits are invariant" (lines 592-595). *Confirms* §§ 1 and 5: met trivially by invariant generics.
- **[Anc-Same-Trait] (Figure 4, p. 11:11).** `T[[γ]] ∈ {J}`, `Δ ⊢ T[[γ]] <: T[[α]]`, `Δ ⊢ T[[γ]] <: T[[η]]`. *Confirms* §§ 1 and 4: each number type and each extender of the family at one instance.
- **The existential reading and [E-Sub] (§ 4.2, p. 11:12; Figure 6, p. 11:14).** `dom(d) = ∃[[K]](α)`; "an existential type ∃[[K]]α is a subtype of another existential type ∃[[K']]α' if there exists a substitution σ for the type parameters bound in K' that makes σα' a supertype of α" (lines 624-626, continued on p. 11:13). [E-Sub]'s premises: `Δ' = Δ ∪ {{χ} <: P <: {η}}`, the left side's parameters bound as constants; `σ = [γ/Q]`, `γ ≠ Bottom`, σ within `Q`'s bounds; `Δ' ⊢ α <: σα'`. Existential subtyping `⊑` first reduces the left side (Figure 6, "Existential subtyping"), which changes nothing for a domain without parameters. *Sharpens* § 4: one domain is below another by one substitution for the right side's parameters, found after the left side's are opened as constants. That is the premise row 682 turns on (§ 7.2).
- **[Meet-Excl] and existential reduction (Figure 5; pp. 11:13-14).** `Δ ⊢ (dom(d) ⊓ dom(d')) ⊑ ∃[[]]Bottom`; the reduction "first collects constraints C that make α different from Bottom" (lines 733-736). The worked `ArrayList`/`List` case takes its exclusion from [Anc-Same-Trait] under invariance: "any subtypes of theirs are exclusive unless they are both ArrayList[[S]] for some type S" (p. 11:13, lines 681-683). *Sharpens* § 2: in FGFV two instances of one invariant trait at different arguments exclude, and an object excludes what it does not extend; two unrelated traits never do, since nothing forbids a class extending both. The block's pairs need `Array[\T,I\] ⊓ T'` empty for every number type `T'`, which only `Number`'s closure gives; § 2 stands with "two traits never exclude" read as "two unrelated traits".
- **The static return type at run time (§ 5.1, pp. 11:16-17).** "the static types of method invocation expressions must be available at run time" (lines 820-822); [T-Method] annotates `ε.m(ε'): ρ` (Figure 7); [R-Method] carries `g'` (Figure 8); "A ground type g is a dynamically available type, which is an internal type that does not contain type parameters nor Bottom" (lines 844-846); "all the type parameters are instantiated with ground types at run time" (line 884). *Confirms* § 3's clause for phase 5, and *sharpens* it: by Figure 8's grammar a type holding an opened size is no `g`, and the paper's static types never hold an opened variable, so [R-Method] never meets the case; the completion from the argument's descriptor is the revival's addition, as § 3 says.

- **[Return-Test] (Figure 5, p. 11:13; p. 11:15).** Premises `Δ ⊢ dom(d) ⊑ dom(d')` and `Δ ⊢ ∀[[κ]](α → ρ) ⊑ ∀[[κ, κ']]((α ⊓ α') → ρ')`; the prose, "[Return-Test] ensures that for any instance of d2 instantiated with σ2 that is applicable to γ, there exists an instance of d1 instantiated with σ1 ∘ σ2 ∘ σ that is applicable to γ and has a return type that is a subtype of the return type of the instance of d2" (lines 769-771). *Confirms* § 4 (row 690) and § 5.

Objects "are like Java final classes that cannot be extended" (p. 11:8), the premise of § 3's "a trait is below no instance of an object".
- **§ 3's phrase "the paper's static argument types are ground".** A static type is an external type `τ` (Figure 2, p. 11:8), which may name a type parameter in scope; "ground" is the run time's word (Figure 8). What § 3 needed holds: a static type is never existential. *Sharpens* a word; the point stands.
- **The items marked "by reading".** Top-level functions as the paper's receiver-free case: the paper is silent, unchanged. § 4's applicable-set argument for row 682: overturned, below.

### 7.2 Row 682 settled

**The pair.** `f(x: NatParamT)` beside `f[\nat n\](x: Nt[\n\])`, with `trait NatParamT comprises { Nt[\n\] } where [\nat n\]` and `value object Nt[\nat n\] extends NatParamT` (`ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXNatOpenOverloadChecker.fss`). The domains are `∃∅. NatParamT` and `∃n. Nt[\n\]`.

**In the paper's own calculus the pair is valid, and the generic declaration is strictly more specific.** `∃n. Nt[\n\] ⊑ ∃∅. NatParamT`: open `n` as a constant; `Nt[\n\] <: NatParamT` by its `extends`. `∃∅. NatParamT ⊑ ∃n. Nt[\n\]`: [E-Sub] asks for one `γ` with `NatParamT <: Nt[\γ\]`; no ground size serves, since a trait is below no object instance. So [No-Dup-Not-Less] holds for the plain declaration, [Meet-Less] holds for the generic one, and [Return-Test] holds (`String` on both sides; `Nt[\n\] ⊓ NatParamT` is `Nt[\n\]`). The informal rule says the same: the paper's applicable sets are sets of types, "a generic method declaration d is applicable to a type α if there exists an instance D of d that is applicable to α, that is, the domain type of D is a supertype of α" (p. 11:5, lines 246-248), and the type `NatParamT` is in the plain declaration's set and in no instance of the generic one.
